title: Gradient and y = mx + c
sub: You wrote this week: “y = mx … gradients … if the gradient is pointing to the left it is negative.” Nearly! This week: what a gradient really measures, how to work it out from two points, and what m and c tell you. About 20 minutes on screen, then the written paper.
target: AQA gives marks for working. For a gradient, write the change in y and the change in x as a fraction before you simplify, then check the sign against a sketch: uphill is positive, downhill is negative.

sections.sub: Last week: straight lines and coordinates. From memory.

blocks.q: A line passes through (6, 2), (6, −1) and (6, 9). What is its equation?
blocks.why: Look at what the points share: the x-coordinate is always 6. So the rule is x = 6 (a vertical line). Last week this one caught you out: always ask “which number stays the same?”

blocks.q: A is (5, 2) and B is (−3, 8). What is the x-coordinate of the midpoint of AB?

traps.msg: You used 3 instead of −3. Add them with the sign: 5 + (−3) = 2, then halve.

blocks.why: (5 + −3) ÷ 2 = 2 ÷ 2 = 1. Check: 5 to 1 is 4 back, 1 to −3 is 4 back ✓. (The midpoint is (1, 5).)

blocks.q: Where does the line 2x + 5y = 20 cross the x-axis?
blocks.why: On the x-axis, y = 0. So 2x + 0 = 20 and x = 10: the point (10, 0). Check: 2 × 10 + 5 × 0 = 20 ✓. (0, 4) is where it crosses the y-axis.

sections.h: 2. Gradient: how steep, and which way
sections.sub: Read the line from left to right, like a sentence.

blocks.html:
Gradient = how far the line goes up for every 1 across.

From two points: gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. Take the points in the same order on the top and the bottom.

Example: (1, 2) and (3, 8). Change in y = 8 − 2 = 6. Change in x = 3 − 1 = 2. Gradient = [[6/2]] = 3.

The sign: read the line from left to right. Going uphill, the gradient is positive. Going downhill, it is negative. (Your note said “pointing to the left”: every line points both ways, so always read it left to right.)

blocks.q: A line goes through (0, 0) and (2, 6). What is its gradient?
blocks.why: Up 6 for 2 across, so up 3 for every 1 across. [[6/2]] = 3. [[1/3]] is across ÷ up: upside down.

blocks.q: Work out the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 14).

traps.msg: Upside down: it is change in y on top. (14 − 2) ÷ (4 − 1).

blocks.why: Change in y = 14 − 2 = 12. Change in x = 4 − 1 = 3. Gradient = [[12/3]] = 4. Check: uphill, so positive ✓.

blocks.q: Reading from left to right, a line goes down. Its gradient is…
blocks.why: Downhill from left to right = negative. A flat line (like y = 3) has gradient 0.

blocks.q: Work out the gradient of the line through (2, 9) and (6, 1).

traps.msg: Check the sign. y goes down from 9 to 1 as x goes up: change in y = 1 − 9 = −8.
Upside down: change in y on top, change in x underneath.

blocks.why: Change in y = 1 − 9 = −8. Change in x = 6 − 2 = 4. Gradient = −8 ÷ 4 = −2. Check: from (2, 9) down to (6, 1) is downhill, so negative ✓.

sections.h: 3. y = mx + c, and real AQA questions
sections.sub: Two numbers tell you everything about a straight line.

blocks.html:
In y = mx + c:
• m (the number in front of x) is the gradient.
• c is where the line crosses the y-axis: the point (0, c). (Last week: put x = 0 and only c is left.)

y = mx (no c) goes through (0, 0). That is a proportional graph: double x and y doubles too. That is why your class met it with proportional graphs.

Careful: the equation must start “y = …”. If it starts “2y = …”, divide everything by 2 first.

blocks.q: The line y = 4x − 7 has…
blocks.why: m = 4 (in front of x), c = −7, so it crosses the y-axis at (0, −7): x first, and x is 0 on the y-axis.

blocks.q: Which line shows y directly proportional to x?
blocks.why: Proportional means a straight line through (0, 0): no “+ c”. y = 3x + 1 is straight but starts at (0, 1), so doubling x does not double y. y = 3 is a flat line.

blocks.q:
A straight line
• has gradient 5
• passes through the point (3, 7)

Circle the equation of the line.
blocks.why: Gradient 5, so m = 5: only y = 5x and y = 5x – 8 are possible. Check the point: when x = 3, y = 5x gives 15 ✗; y = 5x – 8 gives 15 – 8 = 7 ✓.

blocks.q:
The equation of a straight line is 2y = 3x + 5

Circle the gradient of the line.
blocks.why: Make it start “y = ”: divide everything by 2. y = [[3/2]]x + [[5/2]]. The number in front of x is [[3/2]]. (3 is the trap: that is before dividing.)
blocks.ms: [[3/2]] B1 (worked answer: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive)

blocks.q:
P and Q are points.
The x-coordinate of Q is 4 more than the x-coordinate of P.
The y-coordinate of Q is 5 less than the y-coordinate of P.

Work out the gradient of the straight line through P and Q.

traps.msg: Check the sign: y goes down 5 while x goes up 4, so the line is downhill.
Upside down: change in y on top.

blocks.why: Change in y = −5, change in x = +4. Gradient = −5 ÷ 4 = −[[5/4]] (or −1.25). A sketch helps: across 4, down 5.
blocks.ms: Change in y ÷ change in x, e.g. −5 ÷ 4 M1; −[[5/4]] or −1.25 A1 (worked marking: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive)

blocks.q: Explain what the 3 in y = 3x + 2 tells you about the line, and why the line is not a proportional graph.

points.t: the 3 is the gradient: the line goes up 3 for every 1 across
not proportional because it does not go through (0, 0): it crosses the y-axis at (0, 2), so doubling x does not double y

mark.note: Point to the words before you tick. “It goes up 3” earns the first mark only if it says for every 1 across.

blocks.html: Print the written paper and do it by hand. For every gradient, write the fraction (change in y over change in x) before you simplify, and check the sign. Answers on the last page: mark it yourself, then tell Papa your score.

items: I wrote change in y over change in x, with the points in the same order on top and bottom.
I checked the sign: uphill left to right is positive, downhill is negative.
I made the equation start “y = ” before reading m and c.
I wrote the y-intercept as (0, c).
I checked one answer by putting a point back into the equation.

blocks.q: “The line y = 2x − 1: what does the 2 tell you, and where does it cross the y-axis?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for “it goes up 2 for every 1 across” and “at (0, −1)”. If she says “(−1, 0)” or “(0, 2)”, ask “on the y-axis, what is x?”. Then ask “a line goes downhill from left to right: what sign is its gradient?”

paper.title: Maths Week 6: gradient and y = mx + c (written)
paper.sub: Ember · Calculator allowed · about 20 minutes · 16 marks
paper.intro: Skill: written method and checking. For every gradient, write change in y ÷ change in x as a fraction first. Then check the sign against a quick sketch.

blocks.q:
1. Work out the gradient of the straight line through
(a) (1, 3) and (5, 11)
(b) (−1, 4) and (3, −8)
2. Work out the gradient of the straight line through (–2, 3) and (1, 9)

blocks.stem:
3. A is the point (2, –5)
B is the point (4, –9)
blocks.q: Show that the gradient of the straight line passing through A and B is –2

4. Write down the gradient and the coordinates of the y-intercept of each line.
(a) y = 5x + 2     (b) y = 7 − 2x     (c) y = x

5. (Challenge) A straight line has gradient 4 and passes through the point (5, 23)

Work out the equation of the line.
Give your answer in the form y = mx + c

6. Sam says, “y = 2x + 1 is a proportional graph, because it is a straight line.”
Is Sam right? Explain your answer.

selfcheck: Q1–Q3: I wrote the fraction (change in y over change in x) before simplifying.
Q1(b): I checked the sign with a sketch: downhill, so negative.
Q4(b): I spotted that the gradient is the number in front of x, wherever it is written.
Q5: I put x = 5 and y = 23 into y = 4x + c to find c.
Reflection: which question did a sketch help with most?

marking.html:
• 1. (a) (11 − 3) ÷ (5 − 1) = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 (M1 A1). (b) (−8 − 4) ÷ (3 − (−1)) = −12 ÷ 4 = −3 (M1 A1). A positive answer to (b) loses the A mark: the line goes downhill.
  • 2. (AQA Nov 2020 2H Q12) (9 − 3) ÷ (1 − (−2)) = 6 ÷ 3 (M1); = 2 (A1). (Worked marking: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive.)
  • 3. (AQA June 2017 1H Q17(a)), official mark scheme B2: (−9 − (−5)) ÷ (4 − 2) = −4 ÷ 2 = −2, or “change in y ÷ change in x” with −4 and 2, or a triangle drawn with points A and B and side lengths 4 and (−)2 identified. You must show the working: “−2” on its own is already given in the question.
  • 4. (a) gradient 5, (0, 2). (b) gradient −2, (0, 7). (c) gradient 1, (0, 0). (1 each part, both answers needed.)
  • 5. (AQA June 2019 3H Q12), official mark scheme: 4 × 5 + c = 23 M1; c = 3 A1; y = 4x + 3 A1. (SC1 for y = 4x + c with the wrong c.)
  • 6. No (1, with a reason): a proportional graph must go through (0, 0), but y = 2x + 1 crosses the y-axis at (0, 1); for example x = 1 gives y = 3 but x = 2 gives y = 5, not double (1).
